newsitem.title: USA: OUTLOOK-World food supply seen under pressure.
newsitem.headline: OUTLOOK-World food supply seen under pressure.

text.p: Rapidly rising incomes and a growing taste for meat in some developing countries should put additional pressure on world grain production during the next few years, said Christopher Goldthwait, General Sales Manager for the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

"Strong demand pressures are now being generated by rapidly rising incomes, especially in the developing nations of Asia, and by increasing urbanization as more people in developing countries leave the farms to migrate to cities," he said in papers released at USDA's annual agricultural outlook forum.
"The growing taste for meat in developing countries puts substantial additional pressure on world grain production," he added.
Goldthwait also noted food aid availabilities were currently at a 20-year low, reflecting severe budget constraints and reduced stock levels in the traditional donor countries.
World population is also growing at a rate of 80 million people a year, almost all of which is occuring in the lower-income developing countries, many of which are net food importers, he said.
Goldthwait said the rate of growth in world food supply has slowed and agriculture has become more dependent on yield increases with less new land available to bring into production.

"Almost all the gains in food production over the last 20 years have come from genetically improved crops," he said, noting the Consultative Group of International Agricultural Research had estimated new corn varieties emerging from biotech research could feed an additional 50 million people a year.
Goldthwait said although safety must always be a primary consideration, nations needed to use "sound science." There were real risks of not taking advantage of the benefits, he noted.

"In the case of biotech foods these risks may fall disproportionately on the world's poorest nations. People should not be asked to go hungry for want of a higher yielding variety of corn, when all the evidence tells us it is as safe to produce and consume as any traditional hybrid," he said.
